1	From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping
2	LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content
3	Monitoring
4	Yang Li1,2, Qiang Sheng1, Yehan Yang1, Xueyao Zhang3, and Juan Cao1,2
5	1Media Synthesis and Forensics Lab, Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences
6	2University of Chinese Academy of Sciences3The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
7	Warning: this paper may contain potentially generated harmful content.
8	Though safety alignment has been applied to most large language models (LLMs), LLM service providers
9	generally deploy a subsequent moderation as the external safety guardrail in real-world products. Existing
10	moderators mainly practice a conventional full detection, which determines the harmfulness based on the
11	complete LLM output, causing high service latency. Recent works pay more attention to partial detection
12	where moderators oversee the generation midway and early stop the output if harmfulness is detected, but
13	they directly apply moderators trained with the full detection paradigm to incomplete outputs, introducing a
14	training-inference gap that lowers the performance. In this paper, we explore how to form a data-and-model
15	solution that natively supports partial detection. For the data, we constructFineHarm, a dataset consisting of
16	29K prompt-response pairs with fine-grained annotations to provide reasonable supervision for token-level
17	training. Then, we propose thestreaming content monitor, which is trained with dual supervision of response-
18	and token-level labels and can follow the output stream of LLM to make a timely judgment of harmfulness.
19	Experiments show that SCM gains 0.95+ in macroF1 score that is comparable to full detection, by only
20	seeing the first 18% of tokens in responses on average. Moreover, the SCM can serve as a pseudo-harmfulness
21	annotator for improving safety alignment and lead to a higher harmlessness score than DPO.
22	Date: September 19, 2025
23	Project: https://liesy.github.io/SCM
24	Venue: NeurIPS 2025
25	1. Introduction
26	Large language models (LLMs) that utilize the autoregressive paradigm have demonstrated remarkable
27	capabilities across diverse tasks, playing increasingly important roles in multiple applications (Zhao et al.,
28	2023). However, potential safety risks such as harmful content generation still remain key concerns for
29	stakeholders (Wen et al., 2023, Li et al., 2024). LLMs may fail to refuse to output harmful content, no matter
30	whether they are induced by well-designed malicious prompts or just receive benign requests, which may
31	cause undesirable societal consequences (Chao et al., 2023, Deng et al., 2024, Liu et al., 2024, Yuan et al.,
32	Jin et al., 2024).
33	To mitigate harmful outputs, safety alignment techniques are applied to enhance LLMs’ intrinsic capability
34	of refusing harmful outputs (Bai et al., 2022, Rafailov et al., 2023, Yuan et al., 2025), but current alignment
35	still cannot maintain helpfulness without trading harmlessness, leaving harmful output risks unsolved (Tran
36	et al., 2025, Greenblatt et al., 2024, Qi et al., 2025). This necessitates the equipment of a content moderator
37	as the second safety guardrail for LLM services in real-world production environments, which oversees
38	Email(s): {liyang23s,shengqiang18z,caojuan}@ict.ac.cn
39	arXiv:2506.09996v3  [cs.CL]  22 Sep 2025
40	From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring
41	Figure 1:Paradigm differences between the existing harmful content detectors and our proposed Streaming Content
42	Monitor (SCM). (a) Existing ones take the complete output of LLMs as input, which leaks harmful outputs to users
43	before the withdrawal (if outputting immediately) or causes additional service delay (if outputting after detection).
44	(b) Differently, SCM works in parallel with the streaming autoregressive generation and stops harmful content midway.
45	Output tokens are inblue shaded boxes. Color depth change fromLookto filthystand for the increasing number of
46	detected harmful tokens in SCM while benign tokens are ingreen shaded boxes.
47	LLM-user interactions and checks whether LLM-generated outputs conform to the corresponding safety
48	specifications before they are delivered (Dong et al., 2024, AWS, 2024, Jarvis, 2023).
49	The existing moderation paradigm primarily fall into thefull detection, which executes in a post-hoc manner,
50	i.e., determining the harmfulness after receiving the complete LLM output. This aligns with conventional
51	content moderation applied to human-written contents, where moderators are trained using complete text
52	pieces based on encoder-only or decoder-only language models (Eskelinen et al., 2023, Logacheva et al., 2022,
53	Lin et al., 2023) and some have been developed as online services (e.g., Google Perspective API (Perspective,
54	2024), OpenAI Moderation API (OpenAI, 2024), and LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023)). Due to their reliance
55	on complete semantics expressed in complete outputs, full detection may cause high service latency.
56	To reduce the impact of service latency on user experience,partial detectionhas received more attention
57	recently, where moderators may interfere with the generation if harmfulness is above the detection threshold
58	midway. For example, ProtectAI (2023) and GuardrailsAI (2023) directly apply moderators trained using the
59	full detection paradigm, where the incomplete LLM response at a certain step is regarded as complete for
60	harmfulness judgment during generation. It undoubtedly reduces the latency and performs a more timely
61	moderation, but it requires repeated encoding of the output content at each step and will cause redundancy
62	costs. More importantly, an inherent gap exists between the training and inference because the applied
63	moderators are intended to make judgments based on complete semantics. This results in a relatively late
64	stopping of harmful outputs as the moderator is better at judging with more complete responses.
65	Ideally, a streaming content moderator for native partial detection is capable of predicting potential unsafe
66	behaviors as early as possible with only incomplete responses available. Though the mentioned works
67	have emerged, there are still challenges for constructing such a moderator:1)How to obtain fine-grained
68	token-level annotations for LLM-generated responses; And2)how to improve the moderator’s capability to
69	predict the potential harmful behaviors with incomplete responses only.
70	2
71	From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring
72	In this paper, we propose a data-and-model solution for constructing a harmful content moderator that
73	natively supports partial detection:1) For data acquisition,we construct a harmful content detection
74	datasetFineHarmconsisting of 29K prompt-response pairs that contain token-level annotations.2) For
75	moderator construction,propose the plug-and-playStreaming Content Monitor (SCM)which is specially
76	designed to work in parallel with the LLM streaming generation, and design hierarchical consistency-aware
77	learning strategy to guide token-level learning on incomplete semantics with future response-level knowledge.
78	Along with the LLM output streaming, SCM fetches the latest token at each step and provides a harmfulness
79	judgment. When the number of tokens that are judged as harmful reaches a preset threshold, this output
80	will be considered harmful and terminated midway. Experiments demonstrate that our proposed partial
81	detection SCM achieves comparative performance (95%+) with full detection models by only seeing the first
82	18% of tokens in responses on average.
83	2. Related Work
84	LLM Harmful Output MitigationTo mitigate harmfulness of LLMs’ output, an intuitive way is to eliminate
85	the harmful instructions before they are fed into the language model, such as detection-based intercept-
86	ing (Alon and Kamfonas, 2023, Jain et al., 2023), perturbation-based filtering (Cao et al., 2023, Robey et al.,
87	2023, Kumar et al., 2023), and system-prompt-based guarding (Sharma et al., 2024, Zou et al., 2024, Zheng
88	et al., 2024). To internalize the safety awareness into LLMs, safety alignment techniques have been widely
89	applied, which fine-tunes the language model to enhance the intrinsic safety guardrails so that the models
90	actively decline to answer harmful requests. Typical techniques include reinforcement learning from human
91	feedback (RLHF) (Bai et al., 2022), direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), and refusal
92	training (Yuan et al., 2025). However, intrinsic guardrails do not always guarantee output safety due to their
93	unstability (Ding et al., 2023, Qi et al., 2025), and once harmful content breaks the safety guardrail, it will
94	be directly displayed to users. In this work, we focus on the inspection of the LLM’s output as an external,
95	final safety guardrail. Some LLM providers like Google, OpenAI, and Meta already offer solutions for content
96	moderation, which enhances safe interactions between LLMs and users (Perspective, 2024, OpenAI, 2024,
97	Inan et al., 2023). More recently, Sharma et al. (2025) propose a constitutional classifier, a framework
98	that trains classifier safeguards using explicit constitutional rules. However, they typically accept complete
99	LLM outputs for harmful content detection and do not natively support streaming detection, leading to low
100	compatibility with the streaming LLM outputting. In this work, we propose SCM, which is specially designed
101	for monitoring LLM outputting streams.
102	Fine-grained Harmful Content DetectionFine-grained harmful content detection (also known as “toxic
103	span detection”) highlights the exact spans in a piece of text that contain harmful elements. Mathew
104	et al. (2021) released a benchmark dataset for hate speech detection on Twitter and Gab with word- and
105	phrase-level span annotations relying on human rationales. SemEval 2021 Task 5 (Pavlopoulos et al., 2021)
106	constructs a dataset of tweets with character-level labels. However, the human text is mostly short (less than
107	200 words), unable to reflect LLM generation preferences, shaping a gap if being directly applied to train an
108	LLM harmful output detector. And the datasets require human annotations, limiting their scalability. Most
109	of the existing harmful content detectors (Zhu et al., 2021, Pavlopoulos et al., 2021, Barbarestani et al.,
110	2022) are fine-tuned based on encoder-only models like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al.,
111	2019), making judgments based on complete semantics by default. In the era of LLMs, an emerging trend is
112	to judge the harmfulness of incomplete LLM response at a certain step to offer fine-grained feedback more
113	timely. Several works (ProtectAI, 2023, GuardrailsAI, 2023) directly apply detectors having been trained
114	on complete response data, introducing an inherent training-inference gap. Therefore, it is of urgent need
115	3
116	From Judgment to Interference: Early Stopping LLM Harmful Outputs via Streaming Content Monitoring

118	respectively.%HarmSentand%HarmWordare the proportion of harmful sentences and words in responses, respectively.

122	to design a more scalable fine-grained LLM-generated data acquisition solution and a training strategy of
123	detectors that enables them to perform harmfulness judgments based on incomplete semantics in LLM output
124	streams, which we tackle by the newly-constructed FineHarm dataset and the Streaming Content Monitor.
125	3. Construction of the FineHarm Dataset
126	We introduce FineHarm, a dataset containing 29K prompt-response pairs for LLM-generated harmful content
127	detection with fine-grained token-level labels. We initially collect 43K+ labeled responses (§ 3.1), and then
128	assign fine-grained harmfulness labels to each token in a heuristic way (§ 3.2).
129	3.1. Coarse-grained Data Collection
130	We collect data by incorporating responses provided by existing datasets and extending it with the uncensored
131	LLM. Generate harmful and benign responses are under our consideration. We collect 8,338 harmful
132	responses and 29,564 benign responses from prompt-response pairs in the WildGuard dataset (Han et al.,
133	2024), covering 9 LLMs (GPT-4, OLMo-7B-Instruct, GPT-3.5, Vicuna-7b-v1.5, Llama3-8B-Instruct, Mistral-
134	7B-Instruct-v0.2, and 3 Dolphin variants). We further divide them into four categories based on whether
135	the prompts used to generate the responses contain harmful intent. To enrich harmful responses, we
136	leverage an uncensored LLM1 to generate new responses for the prompts gathered from WildJailbreak (Jiang
137	et al., 2024) and those that receive benign responses in WildGuard. After the generation, we adopt three
138	renowned services, Perspective API, OpenAI Moderation API, and LlamaGuard, to judge the harmfulness of
139	the generated responses, and determine all response labels using the majority voting of the three models.
140	Finally, the coarse-grained data consists of 14,064 harmful and 29,564 benign responses.
141	3.2. Heuristic Fine-grained Data Annotation
142	To assign token-level harmfulness labels, we first attempted two approaches to locate harmful words, which
143	identify tokens that have large likelihood differences between the uncensored and aligned versions of one
144	LLM, and prompt a strongly capable LLM to identify, respectively. We manually analyzed results from
145	two labeling approaches but found none could provide reasonable fine-grained annotation. We noted that,
146	however, harmful intents correlate more strongly with notional words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) than function
147	words (prepositions,etc.), so we devised a heuristic annotation approach that exploits part-of-speech (POS)
148	tagging to filter function words and label only notional words as harmful. The steps are as follows:
149	1. Split the response into sentences and annotate the sentence-level labels using an LLM.

154	responses that contain at least one harmful sentence, and the benign responses that contain all benign
155	sentences.

157	words. For each sentence judged as benign, we label all the words in the sentence as benign words.
158	The preliminary study on examined annotation approaches is shown in Appendix B, where we find that the
159	POS-based approach is more reliable.

303	5. Experiments
304	In this section, we present the comprehensive experimental results and analysis of the proposed SCM.
305	Additional results are provided in Appendix C.
306	5.1. Experiment Setup
307	BaselinesFrom our knowledge, there are no publicly off-the-shelf partial detection models yet, so we fine-
308	tuned several models with full parameters on the training set of FineHarm to reflect the performance of full
309	and partial detection. We use 3 open-sourced (HateBERT (Caselli et al., 2021), ToxDectRoBERTa (Zhou et al.,
310	2021), and LlamaGuard-3-8B (Inan et al., 2023)) and 2 closed-sourced (Google Perspective (Perspective,
311	2024) and OpenAI Moderation API (OpenAI, 2024)) baselines for full detection. We fine-tuned HateBERT and
312	ToxDectRoBERTa using the same settings as described in their original papers. We also use the pre-trained
313	ModernBERT (Warner et al., 2024) (large; 0.4B parameters) and Qwen2.5 (Yang et al., 2024) (0.5B, 1.5B,
314	and 7B parameters) as the encoders and replace their output heads with an MLP for binary classification.
315	For the full detection, we input the entire response and take the hidden state of the target token in the last
316	layer (the [CLS] token in ModernBERT and the last token in Qwen2.5) as the representation of the entire
317	response to obtain an overall response-level prediction. For partial detection, the prediction of each token is
318	obtained by conducting the full detection based on the cumulative input of all the preceding tokens.
319	MetricsWe mainly use the precision, recall, and F1 scores as the evaluation metrics. In detail, for the full
320	detection, we directly obtain the response-level predictions and then calculate the metrics for both benign
321	and harmful responses. For the partial detection, we first obtain the token-level predictions and then leverage
322	the Delay-k partial detection to determine the response-level prediction as described in § 4.3. The bestk
323	is selected from{1, 2,⋯, 10} based on the validationF1 score. We report the macroF1 score, which is the
324	average ofF1 scores of the benign and harmful responses.
325	Training RecipeOur SCMs take different scales of Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 7B as the base models and
326	replace their output head with the feature extractor and token scorer. For all models, we fine-tune them
327	with full parameters, and the maximum length of the input sequence is set to 4,096 tokens. More details to
328	reproduce the experiments are in Appendix C.

353	Performance: Our partial detection can rival the performance of full detection.Table 2 presents the
354	main results. For ModernBERT, the full version achieves a good detection performance on both benign
355	and harmful responses, which is expected since it is trained on the entire response and can leverage the

357	shows a clear drop due to the inherent gap between the training and inference. For Qwen-2.5, we see a
358	similar trend of performance drop. In contrast, our SCM with Delay-k partial detection shows comparable
359	performance to the full detection on the 0.5B and 1.5B scales and even outperforms its counterpart in the 7B
360	scale. This indicates that SCM can better predict potential harmful responses with only incomplete outputs.
361	The precision of benign responses and the recall of harmful responses are decreased without logic regulation

368	crucial for real-time applications that prevent users from being exposed to complete harmful content. It is
369	worth noting that the worst case is that we detect at the end of the response, which degrades our method to
370	the well-performing but less timely full detection.

471	6. Conclusion
472	We proposed a data-and-model solution to construct a harmful content moderator for large language models
473	followingthepartialdetectionparadigmtoprovideamoreaccurateandtimelyterminationofharmfuloutputs.
474	We constructed the FineHarm dataset with 29K prompt-response pairs with reasonably useful fine-grained
475	token-level annotations based on a heuristic low-cost approach. Then, we designed the Streaming Content
476	Monitor (SCM), a native partial detection method that works in parallel with LLMs’ output streaming. Thanks
477	to the hierarchical consistency-aware learning strategy, SCM learns to predict potential harmful responses
478	with only incomplete responses and supports a flexible monitoring setting that LLM service providers can
479	early stop harmful responses midway. Experiments demonstrate that SCM achieves comparative performance
480	(95%+) with full detection models by only seeing the first 18% of tokens in responses on average, which is
481	crucial for real-time deployments. Moreover, SCM has more potential, exemplified by providing token-level
482	pseudo annotations to successfully improve the effect of safety alignment. We advocate that more attention
483	should be paid to further improving streaming content monitoring for LLMs.

664	A. Discussions
665	From the perspective of content moderation, our SCM provides a solution for constructing an external
666	content moderator that is well compatible with LLMs’ native characteristic of streaming outputting.
667	We update the moderator with an autogressive architecture that natively supports tracking and detecting
668	potential harmful outputs at the token granular and formulate the setting of early stopping action with
669	the Delay-k notations. Besides providing the specific dataset FineHarm and the model SCM, we are more
670	intended to regard this work as an example. LLM service providers, especially those owning an application
671	and having accumulated rich harmful data in practice, can practice their own harmfulness judgment rules
672	using their privately owned corpus with low human annotation required and can update the moderator
673	when needed without fine-tuning the LLM itself (it is even infeasible when an application is built based on an
674	external LLM API). Moreover, such a disentanglement of servicing and moderating enables a more flexible
675	response strategy when harmfulness is detected (e.g., direct refusal (Xie et al., 2025, Yuan et al., 2025),
676	re-generation, model switching,etc.), realizing a more controllable safe content moderation.
677	Even for enhancing LLMs’ internal safety, SCM can also provide assistance.By annotating the safety
678	alignment data with SCM, a reasonably good (though not perfectly accurate) fine-grained token-level
679	annotation is available for safety alignment as a process supervision, which reduces the harmfulness of LLM
680	outputs more than the commonly used DPO. Though this is a side effect beyond our initial intention, we
681	are optimistic that there is more potential in this direction. From the seed pseudo annotated data to the
682	moderator’s annotations, and then to LLMs’ safety alignment, the process described shows an effective and
683	relatively economical solution to expand the scale of safety alignment and improve the LLM safety further.
684	By building an improvement cycle of internal safety improvement and external output moderation, the two
685	complementary ways can build a more comprehensive safety guardrail for LLMs ultimately.
686	Despite the promising results, we still identify the following limitations of this work:1)Although the heuristic
687	annotation approach that we designed for the FineHarm dataset takes advantage of POS information and
688	shows good performance, it may not be able to fully capture all the nuances of harmful content. There
689	could be more complex semantic and pragmatic factors that affect the harmfulness of a response, which are
690	not fully considered in our current annotation strategy.2)The performance of SCM might be affected by
691	the quality and representativeness of the training data. If the training data does not cover certain types of
692	harmful content and real-world scenarios, SCM may miss some harmful outputs or produce false alarms.
693	3)Our exploration of applying SCM in safety alignment is preliminary and not extensive. The token-level
694	DPO signals provided by SCM need to be further optimized and integrated with other alignment techniques
695	to achieve more stable and effective safety alignment. In the future, we plan to explore more effective
696	annotation approaches for token-level harmful signals, more flexible continual training of streaming content
697	monitors, and more efficient reciprocal improvements of both LLMs’ internal safety awareness and external

M Training the Qwen3.6-27B activation
oracle
The Qwen3-8B oracle is the released checkpoint
of Karvonen et al. (2025). For Qwen3.6-27B
no oracle existed prior to this work. We adapt
their LatentQA trainer to a hybrid Gated DeltaNet
(3/4 of token-mixing sublayers) plus Gated At-
tention (1/4 of sublayers) architecture and train
a verbalizer with the same data mixture (system-
prompt question answering, binary classification,
self-supervised context prediction) and the same
LoRA recipe (r=8, one epoch, bf16). Two changes
were needed:
LoRA target selection.The upstream regex
matches only q_proj|k_proj|v_proj|o_proj
and the MLP projections. Those names exist only
in the 1/4 full-attention sublayers of Qwen3.6.
The 3/4 Gated DeltaNet sublayers expose Lin-
ear modules under different names (in_proj_qkv,
in_proj_z, in_proj_b, in_proj_a, out_proj).
Without expanding the regex, LoRA wraps only
one quarter of the token-mixing capacity and train-
ing loss flattens well above the homogeneous base-
line. Our expanded regex covers both attention
types while still excluding the vision tower and
lm_head.
Activation-collection slicing.The upstream
multi-layer activation collector had an off-by-one
in its offset window. We patched the slicing
to honor [max_offset:min_offset] consistently,
which matters when collecting from the trailing
tokens of long inputs.
After these two fixes the verbalizer trains to
comparable out-of-distribution validation loss as
the homogeneous Qwen3-8B oracle (one B200,
≈36 hours wall-clock, single epoch on ≈1 M ex-
amples). The matching secret-word target adapters
are trained with the recipe of section L.
N Hardware, software, and runtime
All runs use a single NVIDIA B200 GPU with
bfloat16 weights. The Qwen3-8B benchmark
sweep completes in ≈8 hours wall-clock; the
Qwen3.6-27B sweep in ≈48 hours; the two
Gemma sweeps and the forced-choice, constrained-
label, and extended-temperature backfills add ≈
70 hours combined. Software: PyTorch 2.11, Hug-
ging Face Transformers 5.8, PEFT 0.19, flash-attn

Different standpoints for cost optimization.Speculative decoding optimizes the single-token generation
stage by replacing the inference of the large LM with the smaller one, while SCM considers the costs in the
overall generation perspective (via stopping the output early by observing fewer tokens, thus eliminating the
unnecessary cost caused by detection after complete outputs). Due to the differences in motivation, the roles
of models, and the standpoints for cost optimization, we believe that the design of SCM is deeply rooted in
the comprehension of harmful output monitoring scenarios and is non-trivial even if speculative decoding
exists.
B. Details on Dataset Construction
B.1. Experimental Results on Data Applied with Different Token-Level Label Annotation Strategies
We have made multiple attempts to obtain the fine-grained annotations:
Directly assigning the response-level label to each token (Direct).We directly assign the labels for each
token according to the harmfulness of the entire response, which is a simple and straightforward method.
For a token, if the response is harmful, it will be labeled as harmful; otherwise, it will be labeled as benign.
Assigning the harmfulness label to the token that has large differences between its likelihoods in
safety-aligned and uncensored LLMs (Diff).Motivated by Lin et al. (2024), we input the harmful response
into both the safety-aligned LLM and its counterpart uncensored one in a teacher-forcing manner and then
calculate the likelihood of each token in the response. The tokens with a large difference in likelihood (here,
0.5) between the two models are considered as harmful.
Locating harmful words using the understanding capability of the strongly-capable LLM (Delete).We
follow Yoon et al. (2024), instructing external strong LLMs (here, GPT-4o-mini) to change the given response
from being harmful to being benign by token deletion only. The deleted tokens are considered as harmful.
We manually analyzed the results labeled with the above approaches, none of which guarantees an acceptable
rationality to a reliable fine-grained annotator. We find that harmful intents are more likely to be indicated
throughthe notional words (such as nouns, verbs, and adjectives), while the function words (such as prepositions,
conjunctions, and exclamations) are less indicative.Based on this assumption, we design a heuristic annotation
approach that leverages the part-of-speech (POS) tagging to filter out function words and only label the
notional words as harmful words.
We use SCM-1.5B as a small-scale model to conduct the preliminary study on those four annotation methods.
Table 5 shows the results of the three methods, and our heuristic method using POS information achieves

=== PAGE 1 ===
Preprint
FAITHFULACTIVATIONVERBALIZATION: REDUCING
HALLUCINATIONS INLLM REPRESENTATIONINTER-
PRETATION
Haiyan Zhao1, Zirui He 1, Wei Shi2, Huiqi Deng 3, Na Zou 2, Mengnan Du 4,∗
1New Jersey Institute of Technology, 2Shanghai AI Laboratory, 3Xi’an JiaoTong University
4Chinese Univerity of Hongkong, Shenzhen
{hz54,zh296}@njit.edu,{shiwei1}@pjlab.org.cn, denghq7@xjtu.edu.cn
zouna891252@gmail.com mengnandu@cuhk.edu.cn
∗Corresponding author
ABSTRACT
Activation verbalization methods such as Activation Oracle and Natural Lan-
guage Autoencoders decode hidden representations of large language models into
human-readable natural language. However, existing methods can produce in-
complete or hallucinated descriptions, making their activation verbalizations dif-
ficult to trust and use reliably in practice. To this end, we introduce A VPO, a
two-stage framework that first reconstructs source text from a hidden activation
and then evaluates the resulting text with a separate frozen question-answering
model, yielding an explicit and inspectable intermediate readout. We further op-
timize the inverter with direct preference optimization (DPO), using rewards that
capture both semantic recoverability and lexical fidelity. Across six text fami-
lies, A VPO improves gist- and detail-level information recovery over the strongest
baseline by up to 17.1 and 9.3 percentage points, respectively. Crucially, the gains
arise from preference optimization rather than fine-tuning on selected reconstruc-
tions alone, enabling compact cross-model inverters to surpass donor-matched
question-conditioned verbalizers while improving both semantic recoverability
and lexical fidelity. Moreover, out-of-distribution case study shows that A VPO
better recovers high-level semantics while fabricating fewer details.
1 INTRODUCTION
Large language models (LLMs) are widely regarded as black boxes, as their computation is carried
out in distributed hidden representations. Decoding these representations into natural language pro-
vides a human-readable view of the information recoverable from them. Recent work suggests that
such representations are more readable than expected: input sequences can be partially reconstructed
from LLM hidden states (Morris et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025), and the semantic information in
activations can be verbalized by a trained decoder (Karvonen et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Pan
et al., 2026). In particular, Activation Oracle (AO) (Karvonen et al., 2026) and Natural Language
Autoencoders (NLA) (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) are two representative examples of methods that
use natural language to interpret the content of LLM representations. Such explanations can make
encoded information directly inspectable by humans, supporting interpretation, error diagnosis, and
downstream analysis without requiring users to reason directly over high-dimensional activations.
Despite this progress, natural-language activation explanations can still be incomplete or factually
inaccurate. For example, given the source text “The 54th Directors Guild of America Awards were
held on March 9, 2002, and hosted by Carl Reiner,” a verbalizer might produce the overly generic
statement “an award ceremony was held,” or a fluent but unsupported claim with the wrong date or
host. These errors respectively lose source-specific information or introduce plausible details un-
supported by the activation, potentially due to imperfect representation–decoder alignment, limited
supervision, information bottlenecks, or the decoder’s language-model priors (Zhao et al., 2026; Li
et al., 2026). They are particularly difficult to diagnose in question-conditioned verbalizers, which
combine semantic readout and answer generation in a single step: when an answer is incorrect, it is
1
arXiv:2609.34033v1  [cs.CL]  27 Sep 2026
=== PAGE 2 ===
Preprint
unclear whether the information was absent from the readout or lost during answering. In contrast,
an explicit intermediate text provides an inspectable readout that can be checked before downstream
question answering, although a failed reconstruction may still reflect limitations of the inverter rather
than the absence of information in the activation.
To this end, we proposeActivation V erbalization through Preference Optimization (A VPO), il-
lustrated in Figure 1, which separates activation verbalization into two stages. In Stage I, a question-
agnostic inverter maps a hidden activation to soft tokens through a Q-Former-style adapter and
reconstructs the source text. Supervised reconstruction treats all tokens equally and gives no signal
about which content matters, so we further optimize the inverter with direct preference optimization
(DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023). Its rewards combine QA-based gist and detail recoverability with an
anchor F1 term over proper nouns and numbers. In Stage II, a separate frozen QA model answers
downstream questions using only the inverted text, without access to the source text or the activation.
We evaluate A VPO on six text families using activations from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-
Small-24B-Instruct-2501, and compare it against training-free and training-based verbalizers un-
der a unified protocol. Although the supervised inverter initially underperforms QA-trained base-
lines, DPO substantially improves its performance, ultimately outperforming the strongest baseline.
A VPO outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 17.1 points on gist and 9.3 points on detail re-
covery. Even a compact Qwen3-4B inverter outperforms donor-matched verbalizers when decoding
activations from larger models. These gains come from preference optimization itself, as fine-tuning
on the chosen responses alone helps only marginally. On out-of-distribution harmful requests and
clinical summaries, A VPO better recovers high-level intent and fabricates patient names far less
often than QA-trained verbalizers. Our main contributions are:
• We introduce AVPO, a two-stage framework for activation verbalization that first reconstructs an
explicit, question-agnostic textual readout from an LLM activation and then evaluates it using a
separate frozen QA interpreter.
• We improve activation inversion through direct preference optimization with rewards for gist-
level recovery, detail-level recovery, and lexical fidelity, enabling compact cross-model decoders
to outperform existing question-conditioned verbalizers.
• Extensive experiments across two donor models, multiple decoder sizes, six text families, and
out-of-distribution settings demonstrate the effectiveness of AVPO, while revealing how repre-
sentation depth, decoder capacity, reward design, and iterative DPO affect inversion quality.
2 RELATEDWORK
Activation verbalization methods provide human-readable interpretations of LLM hidden represen-
tations, including training-free and training-based paradigms.
Training-free Activation V erbalization.Training-free approaches patch a target representation
into a frozen LLM and prompt it to verbalize the encoded information (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024;
Chen et al., 2024), but they neither align the target representation space with the verbalizer nor
adapt the verbalizer to extract the encoded information reliably (Li et al., 2026). More recently,
HARP (Balasubramanian & Feizi, 2026) combines activation-space retrieval with linear operations
and a tool-using LLM agent, avoiding the need to train an explicit activation verbalizer but requiring
a large database of token-level representations from a selected layer.
Training-based Activation V erbalization.In the training-based paradigm, LatentQA (Pan et al.,
2026) fine-tunes LLMs to answer questions about patched activations, while AO (Karvonen et al.,
2026) and its extensions (Bauer et al., 2026) combine activation patching and steering to train verbal-
izers. Adapter-based methods such as Rep2Text (Zhao et al., 2025) and UA V (Zhao et al., 2026) map
activations into decoder-compatible representations with MLP (Liu et al., 2023) and Q-Former (Li
et al., 2023) adapters, enabling cross-model transfer. However, these question-conditioned verbaliz-
ers entangle information readout with answering, making the encoded information difficult to sepa-
rate from the decoder’s prior knowledge, and their teacher-forced training provides limited feedback
on verbalization quality. NLA (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) adds reconstruction feedback by jointly
training a verbalizer and reconstructor, but reconstruction may capture only coarse gist or rely on
private codes rather than validate individual claims (Dingeto, 2026).

A VPO addresses these limitations from both directions. Unlike question-conditioned verbalizers, it
produces a question-agnostic textual readout for the interpreter model to answer questions, so the re-
covered information is inspectable and separated from the interpreter’s prior knowledge. Moreover,
it optimizes the inverter with preference pairs scored by designed rewards, providing sequence-level
feedback on both semantic recoverability and lexical fidelity.
3 METHODOLOGY
OurA VPOframework consists of two stages. Stage I trains a question-agnostic inverter through
supervised reconstruction followed by preference optimization. Stage II evaluates the resulting in-
verted text through downstream question answering with a separate QA model.
3.1 PROBLEMSTATEMENT
Given an input textx= (x 0, . . . , xT−1 ), we feed it into a frozen donor modelMand take the
hidden state of the final non-padding token at layerℓ,h ℓ(x)∈R dh, whered h is the hidden dimen-
sion ofM. Activation verbalization aims to describe the information encoded inh ℓ(x)in natural
language. Existing training-based verbalizers are typically question-conditioned: a single model
directly generates an answera∼p(· |h ℓ(x), q)to a questionq, entangling readout and answering.
We instead separate the two steps. An inverter, consisting of an adapterA ϕ and a decoderG θ, first
reconstructs a textˆx∼π θ,ϕ(· |hℓ(x))without seeing any question, and a separate QA model then
answersqfromˆxalone. Here,ϕandθdenote the adapter and decoder-side LoRA parameters.
3.2 STAGEI: TEXTINVERSION
We adopt the Q-Former-style cross-attention adapter used in UA V (Zhao et al., 2026) to map hidden
representations from a donor model into continuous prefixes in the embedding space of an inverter
model. This adapter explicitly accommodates differences in hidden dimensionality and representa-
tion spaces between the donor and inverter models.
Inverter Model.We implementA ϕ as a Q-Former-style adapter. It projectsh ℓ(x)intoM= 8
activation-dependent context slots, whichK= 64learnable queries attend to throughLcross-
attention layers, producing a soft-token prefixS h =A ϕ(hℓ(x))∈R K×d in the decoder’s embed-
ding space. Full equations are given in Appendix A.3.
Supervised Inversion Objective.We use a fixed inversion instruction, “What does this repre-
sentation encode?”, denoted byp inv. LetE(·)denote the decoder’s token embedding lookup ap-

Although supervised inversion teaches the inverter to reconstruct the source sequence, token-level

Reward Components.Given an inputxand its inverted sequenceˆx, we evaluate whetherˆxsup-

retaining key tokens from the input. We extract proper nouns and numbers fromxandˆxas anchors
and compute the F1 score between the two anchor sets (Appendix E.2). This reward directly favors
retaining specific names and numbers while penalizing unmatched anchors in the inverted sequence.

4 EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we first describe the experimental setup (§4.1) and then compare A VPO with exist-
ing activation verbalizers on both in-distribution (§4.2) and out-of-distribution (§4.6) datasets. We
further examine how inversion quality depends on the reward design (§4.3), the representation depth
(§4.4), and iterative preference optimization (§4.5). Additional analyses, including the effect of
decoder size, are provided in Appendix G.

4.1 EXPERIMENTALSETUP
Language Models and Comparing Baselines.We verbalize last-token activations from Llama-
3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, using either the donor itself (self) or a smaller
cross-model decoder (Qwen3-4B or Qwen3-0.6B) as the inverter. Reward ablations use layer-27
activations of Qwen3-4B decoded by Qwen3-4B. We compare with training-free verbalizers, Patch-
scopes (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024) and SelfIE (Chen et al., 2024), and training-based verbalizers,
LatentQA (Pan et al., 2026), AO (Karvonen et al., 2026), and UA V (Zhao et al., 2026), all rerun on
our data under a unified protocol provided in Appendix D.
Datasets.We construct a corpus from six English text families: Wikipedia (Wikimedia Founda-
tion, 2023), AG News (Zhang et al., 2015), peS2o scientific text (Soldaini & Lo, 2023), affective
text from SST-2 (Socher et al., 2013), DAIR Emotion (Saravia et al., 2018), and TweetEval (Barbieri
et al., 2020), LMSYS-Chat-1M user turns (Zheng et al., 2024), and LatentQA control prompts (Pan
et al., 2026). Each text is limited to 64 tokens and paired with one gist and one detail QA pair gener-
ated by Qwen3-14B (Qwen Team, 2025b). The corpus contains 165,760 training, 2,172 validation,
and 1,560 test texts, with validation and test sets balanced across families. Preprocessing, filtering,
and deduplication details are provided in Appendix C.
Implementation Details.We first train the inverter with supervised reconstruction and then apply
DPO from this checkpoint. Ablations use a single DPO round, while the main comparison uses
up to six rounds with validation-based checkpoint selection. In each DPO round, we sample eight
candidate reconstructions per training input, rebuild preference pairs using the reward in Eq.( 2),
and use the preceding checkpoint as both the initialization and reference policy. We train DPO
withβ= 0.1, a learning rate of1×10 −5, and family-balanced preference data. Qwen3-32B (Qwen
Team, 2025a) serves as the interpreter and judge for gist and detail scores and also provides the DPO
rewards; for baselines, it scores their direct answers against the source text. In addition to these QA-
based scores, we directly measure the reconstructed text before any question answering: Anchor F1
for proper-noun and number overlap with the source, and within- and cross-output collapse rates
for repetitive and duplicated outputs. The out-of-distribution case studies are scored by GPT-4.1-
mini (OpenAI, 2025). Further details are provided in Appendices B, E.2, E.3, and E.4.
4.2 PERFORMANCECOMPARISON WITHBASELINES
To evaluate whether question-agnostic text inversion can recover information from hidden activa-
tions as effectively as methods directly optimized for downstream question answering, we compare
A VPO with training-free verbalizers, Patchscopes and SelfIE, and training-based verbalizers, UA V ,
AO, and LatentQA. For all methods, we report results at their best-performing layer, and the com-
plete layer-wise evaluation is provided in Appendix G.6.
As shown in Table 1, the SFT inverter initially underperforms several question-conditioned base-
lines. One possible explanation is the difference in training objectives. These baselines receive
direct QA supervision, which explicitly indicates which information in the activation is useful for
downstream questions. In contrast, our SFT inverter is trained only to reconstruct the source text
and receives no signal about which information to prioritize. This objective mismatch may make su-
pervised reconstruction less aligned with QA-based evaluation, even when the relevant information
is present in the activation.
A VPO substantially improves the recovered information. With Qwen3-4B as a cross-model decoder
for Llama-3.1-8B activations, the overall score increases from 0.389 after SFT to 0.472 after one
DPO round and to 0.624 at the validation-selected checkpoint, surpassing AO at 0.423, LatentQA
at 0.475, and UA V at 0.492. The cross-model Qwen3-4B inverter also slightly exceeds our Llama-
3.1-8B self-decoder at 0.608, showing that strong activation readout does not require the decoder
to match the donor model. This pattern is even more pronounced for the larger Mistral-Small-24B
donor. Before DPO, the Qwen3-4B inverter reaches 0.411 overall, below both the Qwen3-4B UA V
baseline at 0.433 and the donor-matched LatentQA at 0.516. A VPO raises the same inverter to
0.638, indicating that DPO can close and reverse the gap between a compact external decoder and
donor-matched verbalizers.

1	Preprint. Under review.
2	Predict, Don’t React: Value-Based Safety Forecasting for LLM
3	Streaming
4	Pride Kavumba1 Koki Wataoka1 Huy H. Nguyen1 Jiaxuan Li1 Masaya Ohagi1∗
5	1SB Intuitions Corp.
6	{pride.kavumba,koki.wataoka,hong.huy.nguyen,jiaxuan.li}@sbintuitions.co.jp
7	Abstract
8	In many practical LLM deployments, a single guardrail is used for both
9	input and output moderation. Input moderation operates on fully ob-
10	served text, whereas streaming output moderation requires safety deci-
11	sions to be made over partial generations. Existing text-based streaming
12	guardrails commonly frame this output-side problem as boundary detec-
13	tion, training models to identify the earliest prefix at which a response has
14	already become unsafe. In this work, we introduce StreamGuard, a unified
15	model-agnostic streaming guardrail that instead formulates moderation
16	as a forecasting problem: given a partial prefix, the model predicts the
17	expected harmfulness of likely future continuations. We supervise this
18	prediction using Monte Carlo rollouts, which enables early intervention
19	without requiring exact token-level boundary annotations.
20	Across standard safety benchmarks, StreamGuard performs strongly both
21	for input moderation and for streaming output moderation. At the 8B scale,
22	StreamGuard improves aggregated input-moderation F1 from 86.7 to 88.2
23	and aggregated streaming output-moderation F1 from 80.4 to 81.9 relative
24	to Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B-strict. On the QWENGUARDTEST response loc
25	streaming benchmark, StreamGuard reaches 97.5 F1, 95.1 recall, and 92.6%
26	on-time intervention, compared to 95.9 F1, 92.1 recall, and 89.9% for
27	Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B-strict, while reducing the miss rate from 7.9%
28	to 4.9%. We further show that forecasting-based supervision transfers ef-
29	fectively across tokenizers and model families: with transferred targets,
30	Gemma3-StreamGuard-1B reaches 81.3 output-moderation F1, 98.2 stream-
31	ing F1, and a 3.5% miss rate. These results show that forecasting future risk
32	enables effective low-latency streaming moderation without exact bound-
33	ary labels.1
34	1 Introduction
35	Safety guardrails are now a standard component of Large Language Model (LLM) de-
36	ployments, mitigating risks such as harmful instructions and toxic content (Carlini et al.,
37	2023; Wei et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). In practice, a single guardrail is often deployed
38	to handle both input and output moderation, but the two settings differ in observability.
39	Input moderation operates on fully observed text, whereas output moderation in streaming
40	systems requires decisions over partial prefixes before the final completion is available,
41	creating a tension between safety and responsiveness.
42	Text moderators such as LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023) are designed for full-sequence
43	classification and are therefore most naturally applied after generation has completed. In
44	a streaming product, that leaves an undesirable choice: either hold back the response
45	until moderation finishes, increasing latency, or display tokens before the safety decision is
46	finalized, creating an exposure window during which unsafe content may already have been
47	shown. White-box defenses address this problem by attaching classifiers to the generator’s
48	∗Currently at Sakana AI
49	1Upon acceptance, we plan to release the research artifacts associated with this work.
50	1
51	arXiv:2604.03962v1  [cs.CL]  5 Apr 2026
52	Preprint. Under review.
53	Figure 1: Boundary detection versus forecasting in streaming moderation. Top: Boundary-
54	detection methods evaluate whether thecurrent prefixhas already crossed an unsafe bound-
55	ary, so intervention is tied to when unsafe content becomes explicit in the text. Bottom:
56	StreamGuard instead scores each prefix by itsexpected future harmfulness, predicting whether
57	likely continuations are likely to lead to an unsafe completion. This supports early interven-
58	tion in streaming settings without requiring exact token-level boundary annotations.
59	internal activations (Li et al., 2025), but these approaches require access to hidden states and
60	are coupled to particular model architectures and checkpoints, which limits portability.
61	Recent text-based streaming guardrails address this gap by framing moderation as abound-
62	ary detectionproblem: the model is trained to identify the earliest prefix at which a response
63	has already become unsafe. This is a natural formulation, and systems such as Qwen3Guard-
64	Stream (Zhao et al., 2025) provide a strong reference point for streaming moderation. At the
65	same time, exact boundary supervision is expensive to construct, depends on the rollout-
66	and-judge pipeline used to define the boundary, and is tied to tokenizer-specific coordinates.
67	These practical costs motivate a different approach to streaming moderation.
68	In this work, we introduce StreamGuard, a unified model-agnostic guardrail for streaming
69	LLM systems that instead formulates moderation as aforecastingproblem. As illustrated in
70	Figure 1, StreamGuard estimates the expected harmfulness of likely future continuations
71	from the current prefix. We train this predictor using Monte Carlo rollouts: for each prefix,
72	we sample possible futures, score them with a safety judge, and use the resulting future-
73	risk estimate as supervision. A key advantage of this formulation is portability. Because
74	supervision is defined over text prefixes with soft future-risk targets rather than tokenizer-
75	specific boundary indices, the resulting training data transfers naturally across tokenizers
76	and model families.
77	Across our evaluations, StreamGuard delivers strong performance both as an input modera-
78	tor and as a streaming response guardrail. At the 8B scale, StreamGuard improves aggre-
79	gated input-moderation F1 from 86.7 to 88.2 and aggregated streaming output-moderation
80	F1 from 80.4 to 81.9 relative to Qwen3Guard-Stream-8B-strict. On the QWENGUARDTEST
81	response loc streaming benchmark, the 8B StreamGuard model reaches 97.5 F1, 95.1 recall,
82	and 92.6% on-time intervention, compared to 95.9 F1, 92.1 recall, and 89.9% for Qwen3Guard-
83	Stream-8B-strict, while reducing the miss rate from 7.9% to 4.9%. These results show that
84	strong end-to-end streaming moderation can be obtained without exact boundary labels,
85	while retaining portability across model families.
86	Our main contributions are as follows:
87	• We introduce StreamGuard, a unified guardrail for prompt and streaming output
88	moderation, with a forecasting-based formulation for streaming output moderation
89	that provides a model-agnostic alternative to boundary supervision.
90	2
91	Preprint. Under review.
92	• We show that forecasting yields strong end-to-end moderation performance, im-
93	proving both standard input/output moderation scores and streaming unsafe-event
94	detection against a strong published boundary-based reference.
95	• We demonstrate that forecasting supervision transfers across model families and
96	tokenizers, including to Gemma (Team et al., 2025) and Qwen (Yang et al., 2025)
97	backbones, and we provide ablations characterizing how rollout construction, ag-
98	gregation, filtering, and supervision density affect performance and annotation
99	cost.
100	2 Methodology
101	StreamGuard’s core methodological idea is to cast streaming output moderation as aforecast-
102	ingproblem. Given a partially generated response, the model estimates a scalarfuture-risk
103	score: the expected harmfulness of plausible continuations conditioned on the prompt and
104	the observed prefix.
105	2.1 Prefix-Conditioned Safety Value
106	Let x denote a user prompt and let y={y 1, y2, . . ., yT} denote a model response. For each
107	observed prefix y≤t, we define the target value as the expected harmfulness of plausible
108	future completions:
109	V∗(x,y ≤t) =E ˜yt+1:T ∼q(·|x,y ≤t ) [O(x,y ≤t ∥ ˜yt+1:T )] , (1)
110	where q(· |x, y≤t) is a continuation distribution over possible futures and O(·) is a safety
111	judge that maps a completed response to a score in[0, 1].
112	Unlike boundary-detection approaches such as Qwen3Guard-Stream (Zhao et al., 2025),
113	which predict the first prefix that is already explicitly unsafe, we estimate the expected
114	risk of continuing from the current prefix. For example, for“To build a bomb, first you
115	must”, a boundary detector may still predict safe because no explicit violation has yet
116	appeared, whereas our objective assigns a high score if likely continuations are harmful.
117	This framing also avoids propagating the final response label to all earlier prefixes, which
118	would incorrectly mark generic scaffolds such as“I”,“The”, or“This”as unsafe whenever
119	they occur in an unsafe completion.
120	2.2 Monte Carlo Future-Risk Targets

122	Monte Carlo rollouts. For a supervised prefixy ≤t, we sampleMcontinuations

154	StreamGuard predicts a scalar risk score for each observed prefix:

164	main results, we use a fixed reference target-construction setup and analyze rollout-source
165	composition, score aggregation, and supervision density in Section 5.
166	3 Experimental Setup
167	3.1 Datasets and Evaluation
168	We evaluate StreamGuard on input moderation, output moderation, overblocking on chal-
169	lenging benign responses, streaming intervention timing, and transfer across tokenizers
170	and model families. Input moderation is evaluated on fully observed text, while output
171	moderation is evaluated in a simulated streaming setting in which the model processes
172	outputs one token at a time. For input and output moderation, we follow the test-split
173	settings used by Han et al. (2024).
174	Input moderation.We evaluate unsafe-prompt detection on TOXICCHAT(Lin et al., 2023),
175	OPENAIMODERATION(Markov et al., 2023), AEGIS(Ghosh et al., 2024), AEGIS2.0 (Ghosh
176	et al., 2025), SIMPLESAFETYTESTS(Vidgen et al., 2024), HARMBENCH(Mazeika et al., 2024),
177	and WILDGUARDTEST(Han et al., 2024). Following prior guardrail work (Inan et al., 2023;
178	Han et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025), we report F1.
179	Output moderation.We evaluate unsafe-response detection on HARMBENCH,
180	SAFERLHF (Dai et al., 2023), BEAVERTAILS(Ji et al., 2023), XSTEST-RESP(Han et al., 2024),
181	WILDGUARDTEST, and AEGIS2.0. We report F1. All experiments other than input moder-
182	ation use the debounced rule from Qwen3Guard-Stream (Zhao et al., 2025): a response is
183	counted as unsafe after two consecutive unsafe predictions.
184	Overblocking.We evaluate overblocking on XSTEST-RESP. Because it contains benign
185	responses with strong lexical overlap to unsafe requests, it is a stress test for whether a
186	moderator incorrectly flags safe responses based on surface cues. We report false positive
187	rate (FPR) on the benign subset.
188	4
189	Preprint. Under review.
190	Streaming intervention timing.We evaluate on the response loc subset of QWEN-
191	GUARDTEST(Zhao et al., 2025) (813 unsafe responses). The benchmark provides sentence-
192	level onset spans rather than exact onset-token annotations, leaving the precise unsafe onset
193	token undefined. Because the flagged sentence typically begins with neutral scaffolding,
194	treating the sentence start as the unsafe onset is inaccurate. Therefore, we evaluate inter-
195	vention timing against theendof the annotated sentence, the label-supported boundary for
196	timely intervention.2
197	To fairly compare models with different tokenizers, we align evaluations to Qwen prefix
198	steps by incrementally decoding Qwen token prefixes into text. Prefixes failing to decode to
199	valid UTF-8 text are skipped. While this is slightly conservative for non-Qwen models, it
200	ensures a standardized comparison axis. For example, let ei denote the last token position of
201	the annotated unsafe span, and let Ti denote the end of the response. We categorize the first
202	trigger asOnTime(triggers at or before ei),Late(triggers after ei), orMiss(never triggers).
203	Latency.Additionally, we report wall-clock latency for streaming moderation. We measure
204	average guardrail decision time and compare it to the generator’s average per-token latency.
205	Full measurement details are deferred to Appendix E.

212	streaming-timing and overblocking evaluations.3

216	study portability beyond a single tokenizer family, we additionally evaluate transfer to

219	positions or in text space. In the native setting, labels are attached to tokenizer-aligned
220	prefix positions; in the transfer setting, where tokenizer coordinates differ, we reuse the
221	same supervision by pairing decoded text prefixes with future-risk targets. We realize this
222	with a lightweight linear head applied to the hidden state at each observed token position,
223	which yields a risk score for the corresponding response prefix.

227	with mean reduction, a four-model rollout pool, and a fixed supervision schedule. For the
228	reference rollout pool, we sample continuations from Llama 3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024) 8B
229	and 70B, and Qwen2.5 (Qwen et al., 2025) 7B and 72B, drawing four rollouts per model at
230	temperature 0.7. We score these rollouts using Qwen3Guard-8B-strict (Zhao et al., 2025).
231	In these datasets, rollout expansion is only necessary for unsafe prompts, as the unsafe
232	responses present arise specifically from unsafe prompts.

234	training setup uses a budgeted supervision schedule on longer-response datasets such as
235	WILDGUARDTRAIN, applying prefix supervision densely over an initial segment and more
236	sparsely thereafter. We train all variants with three random seeds and report mean and
237	standard deviation across seeds (See Appendix A for details).

390	5 Ablation Studies
391	Table 5 studies three practical target-construction choices with the Llama3-StreamGuard-8B
392	backbone: reduction rule, rollout-source composition, and supervision density. Overall,
393	StreamGuard is robust to these choices. Input moderation changes little across variants,
394	while the main trade-off is between early intervention and better benign calibration.
395	Reduction.Reduction has the clearest effect on operating point. Max reduction gives the
396	strongest streaming numbers (98.1 F1, 95.1% OnTime, 3.8% Miss) but hurts overall output
397	moderation and benign calibration, whereas min reduction is more conservative and lowers
398	FPR at the cost of substantially worse streaming performance. Mean reduction provides the
399	best overall balance and is therefore used as the reference setup.
400	Rollout mix.Rollout-source composition changes the balance between aggressiveness
401	and robustness. Single-model Llama rollouts slightly improve streaming intervention,
402	but mixed-generator rollouts yield better overall output moderation and calibration. This
403	supports using a diverse rollout pool in the reference configuration.
404	Supervision density.Streaming performance is relatively insensitive to supervision den-
405	sity, suggesting that dense labels at every token are unnecessary. A modest dense prefix
406	with a sparse tail preserves the main gains while improving efficiency, and D64 S4 gives the
407	best XSTEST-RESPtrade-off in this block.

410	6 Related Work
411	Full-Sequence Output Moderation.Most deployed guardrails operatepost hoc: they
412	inspect a complete prompt or response after it has already been produced. Models such as
413	LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023) and WildGuard (Han et al., 2024) cast safety as full-sequence
414	classification over a fixed taxonomy of harms. These systems are effective as offline judges,
415	but they do not natively solve the streaming problem because they require the completed
416	response before producing a decision. Recent moderators such as BingoGuard (Yin et al.,
417	2025) and policy-adaptive systems such as DynaGuard (Hoover et al., 2025) and OpenAI’s
418	gpt-oss-safeguard (OpenAI, 2025) increase granularity or flexibility, but they still rely on
419	full context and therefore inherit the same latency bottleneck in streaming settings.
420	White-Box and Internal Defenses.A separate line of work reduces moderation latency
421	by leveraging the generator LLM’s internal activations. ShieldHead (Xuan et al., 2025)
422	and related internal probes attach lightweight safety heads to hidden states, while recent
423	streaming white-box systems such as Kelp (Li et al., 2025) extend this idea to token-level
424	intervention during decoding by reading internal activations online and modeling risk over
425	time. These methods can be fast, but they are architecture-dependent: the detector is trained
426	on the representation space of a particular base model and is therefore coupled to that
427	model family and checkpoint. In contrast, StreamGuard is a text-only guardrail trained and
428	deployed over prefixes in text space, which makes it compatible with standard black-box
429	moderation setups.
430	Streaming Safety Systems.Streaming-specific safety systems are the closest prior work
431	to our setting because they moderate partial output prefixes online. Constitutional Clas-
432	sifiers (Sharma et al., 2025) are conceptually close, as they also train on partial outputs
433	to anticipate eventual harmfulness. However, they use prefix-to-final-label supervision,
434	whereas StreamGuard supervises each prefix with a Monte Carlo estimate of the expected
435	harmfulness of likely future continuations. Because the system is not publicly released, we
436	treat it as related work rather than as a direct empirical baseline. In the open text-based
437	setting, Qwen3Guard-Stream (Zhao et al., 2025) is the strongest directly comparable base-
438	line, with publicly released models; however, it uses a different supervision signal, casting
439	streaming moderation as boundary detection by identifying the earliest token at which
440	the response becomes unsafe, labeling earlier prefixes as safe and the boundary and all
441	later prefixes as unsafe or controversial. StreamGuard differs from both approaches in its
442	training target: rather than assigning each prefix the label of one realized completion or
443	the label induced by an explicit unsafe boundary, it supervises each observed prefix with
444	a Monte Carlo estimate of the expected harmfulness of likely future continuations. As a
445	result, StreamGuard is trained to forecast future risk from the current prefix, not merely to
446	inherit a final-output label or detect that an unsafe boundary has already been crossed.
447	7 Conclusion
448	We introduced StreamGuard, a unified text-based guardrail for input moderation and
449	streaming output moderation. For streaming outputs, StreamGuard treats moderation as a
450	forecasting problem: given a partial prefix, it predicts the harmfulness of likely future con-
451	tinuations rather than waiting until an explicit violation has already appeared. This enables
452	earlier intervention during generation without requiring exact boundary annotations.
453	Across standard moderation benchmarks, StreamGuard remains competitive as a conven-
454	tional moderator while improving over strong published streaming baselines on output-side
455	and intervention-timing evaluations. On the streaming benchmark, it achieves higher overall
456	recall, more on-time interventions, and fewer missed unsafe responses than the comparable
457	boundary-based baseline. We also find that forecasting-based supervision transfers well
458	across tokenizer families, yielding strong output-moderation and streaming performance
459	on Gemma and Qwen backbones. Overall, our results suggest that forecasting is a useful
460	and practical framing for streaming safety: it is simple to train, compatible with text-only
461	black-box moderation, and also effective in low-latency deployment settings.

=== PAGE 1 ===
Paper currently under review
SELECTINGTHEMOSTINFORMATIVETOKENS IN
NATURALLANGUAGEAUTOENCODERS
Federico Torrielli1,∗, Gianluca Barmina2,∗, Andrea Blasi N´u˜nez2,
Amon Rapp1, Luigi Di Caro1, Peter Schneider-Kamp2, Lukas Galke Poech2
1Department of Computer Science, University of Turin, Italy
2Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Southern Denmark, Denmark
∗Equal contribution.
{federico.torrielli, amon.rapp, luigi.dicaro}@unito.it
{gbarmina, abln, petersk, galke}@imada.sdu.dk
ABSTRACT
Natural language autoencoders translate a language model’s internal activations into
readable explanations. Explaining every token position is costly. Which positions
should an auditor inspect to understand a potential threat? We study this question
across 4.7 million explanations on prompt injection and concealment. We compare
signals from model computation with a ranker trained only on chat structure. Chat
structure usually selects more relevant explanations than the computational signals,
without requiring a model forward pass for position selection. On three of four
datasets, explaining just 5% of positions retains nearly all of the success rate from
explaining every position, where success means obtaining an explanation about
the threat. The benefit varies with the audit task. We also show that pretrained
verbalizers recover words that models have learned to conceal through fine-tuning,
without additional verbalizer training. These results identify where auditors can
concentrate explanation generation and show that useful explanations can extend
beyond the model a verbalizer was trained to describe.
1 INTRODUCTION
A long line of interpretability work translates the residual stream into a more legible form that
developers and auditors can use to examine and debug a model (Biecek & Samek, 2024). A newer
family of methods instead prompts (Ghandeharioun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024) or fine-tunes (Pan
et al., 2026; Karvonen et al., 2026; Torrielli et al., 2026b) the model to describe its own internal state
in natural language. Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) use a
natural language bottleneck for reconstructing the original activations: a verbalizer model writes a
short paragraph describing the activation, and the reconstructor maps that paragraph back to a vector.
The verbalizer and reconstructor are trained jointly via reinforcement learning to circumvent the
non-differentiable natural language bottleneck. Appendix A describes related methods in more detail.
Generating an explanation requires an autoregressive generation loop. The verbalizers released by
Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026) generate 130 tokens on average for each activation, with a maximum of
150 tokens. A transcript under audit contains hundreds to thousands of positions. Explaining every
position is therefore impractical for live monitoring (Bowkis & Africa, 2026).
Previous work chooses positions by convention. Hu & Greenblatt (2026) test whether explanations
describe a model’s unspoken reasoning on mathematics problems and read only the final position
before the answer. Bowkis & Africa (2026) read a monitor’s activations to catch reward hacking in
agent transcripts and use eight evenly spaced positions per transcript. They report that explanations
at generic positions describe the local text format. Choosing positions by attention weight did not
improve over an even grid. Both conventions spend the budget on arbitrary positions, potentially
overlooking informative tokens. We call a score computed before any explanation is generated a
ranker: it orders token positions by how likely their explanations are to be relevant to the audit.
1
arXiv:2609.37040v1  [cs.CL]  29 Sep 2026
=== PAGE 2 ===
Paper currently under review
Here, we test thirteen signals from three families: the predictive distribution, the attention pattern,
and the activation vector. All thirteen signals can be produced in a single forward pass, with no
verbalization needed. We evaluate whether these quantities predict if the explanation a verbalizer
generates at a position will describe the threat under audit. Section 2.1 and Appendix I describe the
signals and their mechanisms.
Our experiment links each signal to the outcome of an explanation. We call one such connection a
bridge. We build one bridge for each dataset and model. The four datasets are OpenPromptInjection
and Tensor Trust, covering prompt injection, and Liars’ Bench and the taboo organisms, covering
concealment. We verbalize every token of the transcript, including chat template. An evaluator exam-
ines each explanation alone and answers whether it is about the threat under audit. An explanation
the evaluator accepts ison-task. We measure how well candidate signals rank on-task positions above
off-task ones by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). We validate
selection on separate test transcripts and on each model excluded from selection one at a time.
Our contributions are:
• We provide the first systematic study of NLA position selection across 4,705,657 expla-
nations. The evaluation connects selection scores to explanation relevance at every token
position.
• We compare 247 candidate scores. Signals computed from activation vectors are strongest
among individual signals in 11 of 14 combinations. Combining signals improves ranking on
separate test transcripts in all fourteen combinations.
• We show that chat structure exceeds the best individual signal in AUROC in 12 of 14
combinations. A 5% position budget retains 95.8% of the success rate from explaining every
position on three datasets.
• We show that pretrained verbalizers recover concealed words from models after fine tuning
without additional verbalizer training. The same prompt produces explanations specific to
each model’s concealed word.
2 METHODS
Preliminaries.NLAs learn to translate internal activations of a frozen target model into natural
language while preserving enough information to reconstruct the original activation. They consist of
anActivation V erbalizer (A V), which maps an activationh to a textual explanation e, and anActivation
Reconstructor (AR), which maps the explanation back to an estimated activation ˆh. Training begins
with a supervised warm-start using synthetic explanations from a teacher model. Afterwards, the
A V and AR are jointly optimized so that explanations enable accurate reconstruction of the original
activation, minimizing Lrec =|h− ˆh|22. This objective encourages the explanation to preserve
information contained in the activation. We include more details on NLAs training in Appendix P.
Notation and problem statement.Adatasetis one collection oftranscripts. Athreatis what an
auditor is looking for in a transcript. Ataskis the job given to the model. An injection tries to replace
that task with another one. An auditor who can afford k explanations for a transcript of n positions,
with k≪n , needs a score for each position that is computable before any explanation is generated,
and that ranks the positions whose explanations will describe the threat above the positions whose
explanations will not. This paper measures how well such a score can be computed from one forward
pass, and whether the rendered transcript alone is enough.
2.1 SIGNALS
At each position t, the model exposes three quantities used by the thirteen signals in Table 1: the
predictive distribution pt over the next token; the attention pattern Aℓit of head i in layer ℓ, with ¯Aℓt its
mean over the nh heads; and the residual-stream activation ht at the verbalizer layer, with hLt being
the final-layer activation. We call each coordinate of an activation vector achannel. We write xt for
the token observed at position t, L for the layers of the model, and d for the width of an activation
vector. Asignalis a scalar computed at one position from one of these quantities. All signals require

approximately 130 tokens. We use each signal as a ranking. We fix signal direction separately for
each dataset and model because the direction identifying relevant positions varies across threats.
We consider three signal families with different motivations:predictive distribution signalsmeasure
how many bits the model needs for the next token (Shannon, 1948);attention signalsmeasure where
the model retrieves information, including whether attention moves away from the opening-position
sink (Xiao et al., 2024) and how attention divides between supplied context and generated text (Chuang
et al., 2024); andactivation signalsmeasure the size, concentration, and position displacement of
the residual stream. Five signals form the activation family in Table 1. Three signals measure
vector magnitude and channel concentration ( norm ratio, peak ratio, dominant mass).
Two signals measure displacement between adjacent positions (resid jump, resid jump nla).
Transformers concentrate large activations in a small set of largely input-independent channels
(Sun et al., 2024). Following their work, we define dominant mass as the share of activation
norm inside S, which is the set of channels whose median magnitude exceeds ten times the median
across all d channels, estimated once per model and dataset, while resid jump nla measures
displacement outsideS. We provide additional motivation for each family in Appendix I.
2.2 BRIDGING SIGNALS TONLARELEVANCE
Ourbridgeexperiment measures whether an explanation generated at each token position describes
the threat under audit, linking acandidate, one of the thirteen signals or 234 ensembles, to the
outcome of an expensive explanation. For each dataset and model, we apply the verbalizer to the
residual-stream activation at every position of the serialized transcript, including prompt, response,
and chat-template tokens, following Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026). Using greedy decoding, we produce
one explanationz c,i per position, for4,705,657explanations in total.
A judge receives each explanation alone and answers a fixed dataset-specific yes or no question. We
use DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) at temperature zero. Answers beginning
with y define yc,i = 1, anon-task explanation. All other answers define yc,i = 0. We include all
the questions in Appendix C, and example off-task and on-task explanations in Appendix B. Where
a dataset marks the threat region or labels the transcript by condition, we compare the on-task rate
inside the marked region with the rate outside it. This comparison verifies that NLA explanations
localize the audited behavior, which has to be true before a signal can predict that localization.
2.3 COMBINING AND SELECTING SIGNALS
The three signal families read different parts of the computation, as detailed in Section 2.1, so we test
whether combining two signals ranks on-task positions better than either alone. We call each signal a
componentof the ensemble. Because signals have different scales, for each model and dataset we

Evaluation measures.Our primary measure is precision at a fixed explanation budget: the fraction
of selected positions whose explanations are on-task. We use budgets of one position, eight positions,
1%, 5%, and 10% of a transcript, and compare against the base rate obtained by selecting positions at
random. We also report case-macro AUROC, computed within each transcript and then averaged, and

We evaluate model-best and dataset-shared selection with five-fold validation over whole transcripts.
In each fold we recompute ranks and directions and reselect the ensemble and best individual signal

Models.We use all four open-weight models for which trained NLAs have been released: Qwen2.5-

The parts of a transcript.We format each transcript with the model’s chat template and tokenize
it into a single sequence. We then assign each token two structural labels that are available without
running the model. A token’schat roleidentifies the component of the rendered transcript that
contains it: the chat template, the system message, a user message, the final assistant reply, or an
earlier assistant message. A token’ssegmentidentifies one of three spans. Theinputis the sequence
from its start through the final content token. Theboundaryis the run of chat-template tokens between
the final content token and the reply, and a boundary token’sboundary ordinalis its position within

input and a boundary only.
Baselines.We compare every signal against a random score and two baselines derived from the
transcript. Thepositionbaseline uses a token’s index and the transcript length. Thestructurebaseline
adds thechat roleandsegment, using markers from the chat template. These features can help locate
the threat because each dataset places it in a fixed part of the conversation. Position also affects how
models use context: a model uses content in the middle of a long input less than at its ends (Liu et al.,
2024a). The residual stream at the opening token and at delimiters concentrates in a few channels
whose identity barely depends on the input (Sun et al., 2024; 2026). We trainpositionandstructure
as logistic regressions on the on-task labels from four fifths of the transcripts and evaluate on the
remaining fifth, keeping training and evaluation transcripts separate. Appendix F gives the features of
both baselines. A signal justifies its forward pass only if its AUROC exceeds that ofstructure.
Controls and false discovery rate.Before the benchmark runs, we fixed head disagreement
as the primary signal for Liars’ Bench and Tensor Trust, because that signal had given the best result
in a pilot experiment. We therefore provide the signal as confirmatory, without a correction for testing
many signals. Every other signal is exploratory and is tested under Benjamini–Hochberg control of
the false discovery rate at q= 0.05 . OpenPromptInjection and the taboo organisms are exploratory
throughout, because the input span setting and the secret word setting had no prior result to register.
